title: The Factors That Matter: A Formula for Understanding China’s Use of Force Calculus Over Taiwan
text:
As the United States and China enter a prolonged period of instability and tension, how and under what circumstances China may use force, or, alternatively, be deterred from using force, has become of crucial importance to U.S. policymakers seeking to avoid conflict with the People’s Republic of China (PRC). While the United States can draw on its experience gauging threats and making difficult strategic calculations during the Cold War rivalry with the Soviet Union, the emerging strategic rivalry with China is still in its early stages. The question of how to deter conflict with the PRC will be an increasingly important factor in the strategic calculations in Beijing and Washington, especially in times of heightened instability and crisis between the two powers. This, in turn, raises enormous and complex questions for U.S. policy regarding U.S.-China strategic stability, U.S.-China crisis management, and strategic and conventional deterrence vis-à-vis China.In spite of this emergent challenge, critical gaps remain in the Western understanding of PRC deterrence concepts. Most importantly, and most urgently, there is little understanding of how or why China may be deterred from resorting to military force in the event of a serious confrontation with the United States. To address these critical gaps, this paper explores China’s approach to deterrence in the military and diplomatic domain, in order to inform U.S. understanding of how it might deter China in a crisis or conflict.  In particular, this paper introduces a set of key variables that matter most to China’s leadership in contemplating using force to “reunify” Taiwan with mainland China. This study  develops a methodological formula that can be used by policy-makers and academics interested in understanding what has deterred Chinese leaders from using force against Taiwan, and what might cause China to change its calculus.  

I. The Stakes

The consequences of large-scale military action between the PRC and Taiwan would be immediate, severe, and long-lasting throughout East Asia and globally. The United States might engage on behalf of Taiwan, risking general war between nations with the world’s two largest economies and most lethal armed forces. The last time the world’s largest economies fought an extended war was in the Second World War, over eight decades ago. Since then, military arsenals have become much deadlier and now include nuclear weapons, the United States possessing the second most warheads (behind Russia), and China the third (though far fewer than the United States). In an intense, protracted conflict, military and civilian casualties among the belligerents, their supporters, and others simply caught in the crossfire would likely reach levels not seen since 1945. Additionally, kinetic and cyberattacks against the opposing side’s terrestrial, maritime, and space-based communications, informational, transportation, and energy infrastructures would have crippling economic effects. The collateral disruption of regional and global trade, investment, and finances would be massive, dwarfing the impacts of the two “Oil Shocks” of the 1970s, the Great Financial Crisis of 2008, or the Coronavirus Pandemic of 2020.1Taiwan remains the world’s most important semiconductor choke point, despite years of efforts by the United States and allied countries to diversify chip manufacturing, especially from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC)—the world's leading advanced semiconductor manufacturer. Even with new fabrication plants under construction in Arizona, Japan, and Europe, a conflict over Taiwan would still produce an unprecedented disruption to the global economy because the most advanced manufacturing capacity—and much of the associated packaging and supplier ecosystem—remains concentrated on the island.2Given the enormous potential costs and uncertainty of outcomes, leaders in Beijing, Taipei, and Washington do not desire a clash of arms. Yet all consider worst case scenarios and understandably direct their militaries to prepare for a wide range of contingencies, including the possibility of a full-scale invasion of Taiwan by the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA).

II. The View from Beijing, Taipei and Washington

The coming several years will be pivotal for deterrence across the Taiwan Strait. With two new leaders elected in Washington and Taipei in 2024, prospects for peace across the Strait hinges on the political considerations of how to maintain the precarious “status quo” between China, Taiwan and the United States. In the years to come, U.S. President Donald Trump and Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te will have to confront the challenge of how to maintain the peace, while balancing domestic considerations that may distract from this central goal.3While China’s President Xi Jinping continues to pursue “peaceful reunification” between mainland China and Taiwan, there are indications that China’s population may be losing patience with non-military approaches to achieving Xi’s goal.4 He has emphasized that the mainland seeks peaceful reunification with Taiwan, but has also asserted, “No matter how the situation on the Taiwan island evolves and no matter how external forces try to interfere, the historical trend that China will and must achieve reunification is unstoppable.”5 Neither he nor any of his predecessors have ever renounced the use of force to achieve reunification.6 Thus, a credible military tool provides the mainland with the ultimate coercive leverage.Taipei views Beijing as becoming increasingly aggressive and impatient with Taiwan’s elected leaders, as evidenced by its insistence on not foreswearing the use of force to resolve the Taiwan question and by larger, more destabilizing military exercises around the island. As a result, the Republic of China Armed Forces (ROCAF) are maintaining a force that can deter PRC military action through its capabilities and readiness and, should deterrence fail, be prepared to mount an effective defense.The U.S. military posture is informed by the 1979 Taiwan Relations Act (TRA), which Congress enacted immediately following the termination of official relations with the Republic of China (Taiwan); it includes multiple security-related provisions. Importantly, beyond making available defense articles and services necessary to enable Taiwan to maintain a sufficient self-defense capability, it also requires the United States to maintain the military capacity “to resist any resort to force or other forms of coercion that would jeopardize the security, or the social or economic system, of the people on Taiwan.”7 U.S. Presidents since that time, in their capacity as Commander-in-Chief, have directed the U.S. Indo-Pacific Command (INDOPACOM) to plan accordingly.Thus, while China, Taiwan, and the United States all wish to avoid a military clash, their armed forces are instructed by civilian leaders to be prepared for a wide range of combat contingencies. Taiwan remains one of the most likely scenarios that could draw all three parties into an armed conflict, despite diplomatic efforts to resolve the dispute through peaceful means.

III. A Formula for China’s Calculus for Taiwan Invasion

This leads to the primary focus of this paper: understanding China’s calculus for whether to take the risky and catastrophic decision to use force against Taiwan. This section introduces a basic formula for understanding the macro-level internal and external factors that China and Xi Jinping will likely consider in contemplating using force to “reunify” Taiwan with mainland China. The variables in this formula are divided into two categories: internal and external factors. Internal factors are variables within China’s control and deal primarily with Chinese military capabilities, domestic political and economic stability, and leader legacy. External factors include variables largely, but not completely, outside the control of China and China’s leaders—namely, the role of Taiwan and its identity vis-à-vis mainland China, the role of the United States and its allies and partners, and the military capabilities of the Taiwanese military.This framework, visualized below in Figure 1, argues that a Chinese decision to invade Taiwan would not be driven by a single trigger, but by the interaction of multiple internal and external variables. Internally, Beijing would weigh the PLA’s military readiness, China's domestic stability, and Xi Jinping's political legacy and strategic objectives. Externally, leaders would assess Taiwan's perceived trajectory toward permanent separation, the broader international environment, the likelihood of U.S. military intervention, the willingness of U.S. allies and partners to respond, and Taiwan's own deterrent capabilities.Before examining the eight factors in detail, a brief explanation of the methodological approach is necessary. The variables included in this framework were selected based on two criteria. First, each represents a strategic-level factor that Chinese leaders are likely to assess directly when weighing the costs, benefits, and feasibility of using force against Taiwan. Second, each has the potential to independently alter Beijing's assessment of whether military action is likely to succeed, whether the timing is advantageous, and whether the expected political and military costs are acceptable. Together, these variables capture the principal internal and external considerations that shape Xi Jinping’s decision-making calculus while remaining sufficiently parsimonious to serve as a useful analytical framework for policymakers and scholars.This framework is not intended to be exhaustive. Other considerations, including elite factional politics, economic conditions, nuclear escalation risks, public opinion, technological change, and intelligence assessments may also influence Beijing's decision-making. Rather than treating each as separate variables, the framework incorporates these considerations where they most directly affect the central strategic calculus. For example, economic conditions are reflected primarily through domestic stability, elite political dynamics through leadership legacy and domestic stability, and nuclear escalation through the broader external environment and expectations regarding U.S. intervention. The objective is therefore not to catalog every possible influence on Chinese decision-making, but to identify the principal variables most likely to determine whether Beijing concludes that the strategic conditions for using force against Taiwan are favorable.Put another way, this formula considers what the author regards as the fundamental variables that Xi must account for in this decision, but not all the factors. The author readily concedes that there are dozens, possibly hundreds, of permutations and factors that a leader could take into account in using force in international politics.8 Beijing’s decision-making process reflects a multitude of factors within a fluid, cost-benefit calculation, rather than a binary choice. As the perceptions of Chinese leaders regarding internal and external factors change, so does their perceptions of the costs and risks of escalation. Thus, the framework emphasizes that these variables are dynamic, interconnected, and based on Chinese leadership perceptions rather than objective reality. Therefore, with this context in mind, the below typology is meant to narrow these factors down into eight variables that likely matter most in the cost-benefit calculus of Xi in considering whether or not to use force against Taiwan.

Internal Factors

PLA Readiness (PLA)

The first and most important variable in any Chinese leader’s decision-making calculus is the capabilities and readiness of the People’s Liberation Army (PLA). This factor affects not only capabilities but leadership confidence, timing, and risk tolerance. While the military milestones9 that Central Military Commission (CMC) Chairman Xi Jinping has laid out for the PLA remain explicitly tied to modernization and preparedness, the 2027 goal in particular has been linked to a possible military invasion of Taiwan.10 For Xi Jinping, readiness affects perceived probability of success: if the post-2015 PLA reforms are seen as successful, this would give Xi greater confidence in his military options.11 However, if corruption, training gaps, or command weaknesses persist, Xi may determine that the PLA is not ready to execute a Taiwan contingency, or at least introduce doubt in Xi’s mind.One component of PLA readiness is the quality of personnel. Here, “quality” primarily refers to the operational experience of PLA commanders and their ability to lead troops into battle. A CSIS report indicates that recent purges within the PLA have depleted the PLA’s bench of senior officers with operational experience.12 Other research suggests that purges and retirements have resulted in fewer senior PLA commanders and CMC members with wartime experience, such as veterans who served in the 1979 Sino-Vietnam War.13 This raises questions about whether the PLA’s increasingly thin roster of experienced officers might erode China’s ability to execute a complex, demanding mission such as an invasion of Taiwan.In addition to having experienced commanders, the PLA must be able to conduct joint operations that combine elements from the different services and branches in order for the PLA to prevail in a potential war over Taiwan. In this context, “readiness” is not just a function of troop numbers and platforms, but a composite of several interdependent capabilities. This includes the effective integration of Army, Navy, Air, Rocket, enabled by logistics, cyber and information support forces, to execute a coordinated, multi-domain campaign as complex as an amphibious invasion of Taiwan. Such operations require unity of command and integrated planning, the interoperability of platforms within and across services, delegation and flexibility, and robust command, control, communications, and surveillance systems. Improving the PLA’s ability to conduct such operations was one of the main reasons Xi launched unprecedented organizational reforms in 2015.14However, the PLA faces major obstacles in successfully executing an amphibious invasion of Taiwan. First, transporting the immense number of troops and equipment needed for a successful invasion is difficult for any military to execute. Such an operation would require thousands of ships, aircraft and personnel to be choreographed in such a way to neutralize the Taiwanese armed forces and within a short enough timeframe to thwart intervention from external actors (namely, the United States). Second, Taiwan's geography poses significant defensive advantages. Much of the coastline is mountainous, with limited viable landing beaches. Any invasion force would have to fight through rugged terrain, rivers, and dense urban areas. This is made more difficult by the fact that Taiwan is focused on developing an asymmetric defense to deter an invasion. This includes procuring long-range missiles, increasing its military budget, and conducting urban resilience drills. Finally, the PLA is largely untested in large-scale combat operations. This lack of experience could strain its command structures, operational effectiveness, and morale.15Nevertheless, Beijing has rarely waited for the right conditions before ordering the PLA into battle. In 1950, for instance, Chinese forces intervened in support of Pyongyang in the Korean War, even though China’s economy and society had been devastated by years of civil war. In 1962, the PLA attacked India, even though China’s most senior military officer had recently been purged for questioning Mao Zedong’s disastrous Great Leap Forward. And in 1979, Beijing dispatched an ill-prepared PLA to Vietnam, where Chinese troops suffered significant losses for limited political gains. Now, as then, Chinese leaders may pursue war even if the domestic economic and political conditions appear unfavorable—and even if the PLA is not ready to fight.16

Domestic Stability in the PRC (DS)

The second variable is domestic stability. This is an important factor in this formula for one simple reason: domestic stability is crucial to Xi’s mandate to run the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and his ability to govern the PRC. It is foundational to the party's legitimacy, economic goals, and ultimate control over society. The CCP derives its authority largely from its ability to deliver prosperity and social order. Consequently, without a solid mandate to govern the country, it is highly unlikely that any Chinese leader would entertain a major military campaign, given the potential for domestic instability to spill over into political unrest.Domestic stability can affect leaders’ decision-making to engage in military hostilities in two contrasting ways. One academic theory suggests positive factors in domestic stability, such as an overall stable and growing economy, a satisfied society whose basic needs are largely met, and a leader who holds a strong political mandate over the country, can provide leaders with confidence to resort to using force in select ways. This theory submits that domestic strength is one component of a country’s comprehensive national power that enables risk taking, to include using military force.17 The logic is that a stable domestic situation could provide the necessary foundation to withstand external economic, diplomatic and military pressure—in the form of international sanctions or military intervention from outside powers—that may follow from a military campaign.A second theory holds that heads of state may resort to using force as a means to distract public attention away from societal and economic problems, sometimes called the “diversionary war” theory. This theory argues that vulnerable leaders manipulate foreign policy in order to enhance their domestic political position, to include launching wars of choice. 18 While burgeoning research suggests empirical validity to this theory, the concept is nonetheless a source of debate for scholars, who highlight gaps in evidence that undermines key tenets of this theory.19The common denominator is that domestic conditions influence a leader’s calculus regarding the use of military force. Chinese leaders are therefore likely to consider domestic stability when deciding whether to use force against Taiwan.

Leadership Legacy (LL)

The third and last variable in the internal factors section considers the role of political legacy. In particular, the extent to which achieving “reunification” with Taiwan would cement a Chinese leader’s mark in the annals of CCP history. During a 2019 speech marking the 40th anniversary of the “Message to Compatriots in Taiwan,” for example, Xi Jinping said, “The long-standing political differences (over Taiwan) should not be allowed to be passed down from one generation to the next.”20 His remarks suggested that patience for “resolving” the Taiwan question is not infinite, and that Xi may prefer to achieve resolution during his tenure as leader of the CCP.Xi’s statement reveals an important variable for PRC leadership about Taiwan—that political resolution of the “Taiwan question” is of great importance to the legacy of individual leaders of China. Every supreme Chinese leader since Mao has desired to bring Taiwan back into the fold, including getting dangerously close to war during three military crises in the 1950s involving Taiwan and the United States.21 But with his rhetoric, Xi appears to have elevated the resolution of the Taiwan question to an even higher priority than previous PRC leaders. Thus, for Xi, settling the Taiwan question on his watch would affirm Xi’s status within the pantheon of Chinese leaders before him who have attempted and failed to unify Taiwan with the mainland.

External Factors

Intent of Taiwan to Permanently Seek or Hold a Separate Status from Mainland China (I)

The first external factor considers Chinese leaders’ assessments of whether Taiwan is on a “permanent course” of separation from mainland China, and whether that trajectory makes the use of force is necessary. Xi has repeatedly emphasized in major speeches on Taiwan the “inevitability” of Taiwan eventually being “reunified” with the mainland, saying, for example, “The historical trend toward a stronger China, national rejuvenation, and reunification cannot be stopped by any force or anyone.”22 For Xi and CCP, Taiwan’s “separation” from the mainland is a legacy of the Chinese civil war that must be resolved through the eventual reunification of Taiwan with mainland China, either peacefully or through force.This factor has taken on added significance in recent years. The ties between the CCP and the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) have weakened significantly since President Lai Ching-te became president in May 2024. Owing to Lai’s unwillingness to affirm Beijing’s “One China Principle” or repeat the “1992 Consensus,” Beijing has shut down virtually all mechanisms of communication with Lai and the DPP.23 Cross-Straits ties have become a key domestic policy issue for both Xi Jinping and Lai, with domestic constituencies on both sides paying greater attention to trends than in the past. On the economic front, since former President Tsai became president in 2016, but especially since Lai took over, Taiwan has embarked on its own “derisking” policy towards mainland China.24 As a result, cross-Strait trade and investment flows have shrunk dramatically over the past five years. While the PRC is keen to use economic ties to bolster cross-Strait integration, Taiwan is moving in the opposite direction. Finally, while social ties between Taiwan and mainland China have been historically close, in particular with Fujian province, where many mainland Chinese fled from during the Chinese civil war, those bonds are diminishing.25From China’s perspective, Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te has arguably taken Taiwan further down a path of “separation” from mainland China. For example, he has stated more unequivocally than previous Taiwanese presidents that Taiwan is “of course” a country, and has labeled the mainland a “foreign hostile force” during a series of speeches aimed at addressing Taiwan’s domestic and international challenges.26 Lai also instituted 17 national security measures to combat PRC espionage, among other initiatives.27 As a result of these policies, Taiwan has severely restricted cross-Strait exchanges, reinstated military tribunals, expelled mainland spouses who advocate for reunification by force, and launched a failed recall campaign against opposition lawmakers. To some observers in China, this trajectory has already crossed Beijing’s “red lines,” forcing China to respond with pointed public condemnation and military exercises.28Within this factor, a key issue is the emergence of a “Taiwanese identity.” A growing proportion of Taiwan's population has come to identify primarily as “Taiwanese” rather than Chinese, a trend that many scholars and policymakers in Beijing view as one of the most consequential long-term challenges to the prospects for peaceful unification.29 From the perspective of Chinese leaders, the gradual strengthening of a distinct Taiwanese identity may indicate that the political and societal foundations for eventual reunification are eroding, narrowing the perceived window of opportunity to resolve the Taiwan issue on Beijing's preferred terms. At the same time, Taiwan’s domestic political landscape constitutes an important variable in Chinese decision-making. The differing approaches of the Kuomintang (KMT), which generally favors closer cross-Strait engagement while opposing formal independence, and the DPP, which emphasizes Taiwan’s separate political identity and sovereignty, shape Beijing’s assessment of the island’s long-term trajectory.30Equally significant is Taiwanese public opinion on unification, independence, and maintenance of the status quo. Recent trends indicate that most Taiwanese people do not support reunification, with the vast majority preferring to “maintain the status quo indefinitely,” “maintain the status quo, decide at a later date,” or “maintain the status quo, move towards independence.”31The above trends are of great concern to China and Xi, because the existence of a separate, sovereign state outside of the PRC challenges Xi’s core goal that Taiwan will “inevitably” be reunified with mainland China. Thus, these variables collectively serve as crucial enabling factors that may change Xi’s calculus regarding whether Taiwan is on a permanent path of separation from mainland China. If Xi concludes, for example, that all prospects for peaceful reunification are narrowing or have closed, he may turn to military force to compel Taiwan to “reunify” with the PRC.

External Events (EE)

The second external factor considers how external events might shape Xi’s assessment of the risks and rewards of military action against Taiwan. Two categories of events are significant: 1) major geopolitical crises or wars that change the risk-reward calculus; and 2) major changes in Taiwanese or U.S. policy toward Taiwan.On the first point, events like the war in Ukraine provide pivotal geopolitical inflection points to reassess the risks and benefits of contemplating using military force against Taiwan. China views the Ukraine war through the lens of U.S. hegemony, using it to refine Beijing’s strategies for potential conflict with Taiwan and how regional countries may respond. China has focused keenly on battlefield developments related to speed, autonomous systems, and non-kinetic warfare to assess trends in warfare. Recent conflicts in Iran and Venezuela also provide data points on warfare and international responses.32 While acknowledging differences between the scenarios, Beijing is studying these conflicts to ensure a swift, decisive victory over Taiwan to mitigate international intervention and domestic risks.On the second point, the two external events most likely to shape Xi’s calculus and prompt him to contemplate military action against Taiwan are 1) a formal declaration of independence by Taiwan; and 2) a fundamental change in the United States’ “One China” policy over Taiwan. The first scenario sees Taiwan under Lai Ching-te formally declaring independence, either through a referendum vote, or through a public statement from President Lai. This would entail Lai taking the extraordinarily risky gamble of legally enshrining Taiwan as a sovereign, independent state in the international community. Lai would only undertake such a move if he believed doing so would serve Taiwan’s interests, or if he felt compelled to do so for domestic political reasons.The second scenario sees Washington changing its “One China” policy to include formally recognizing Taiwan as an independent state and undertaking official exchanges with Taiwan. While the extreme scenario could be formal diplomatic recognition by Washington, there are other less-extreme measures that Donald Trump could take that would signify a major change to U.S. policy that would be considered destabilizing from Beijing’s perspective. This includes an official visit by Trump to Taiwan, or Lai to the United States, for example, or something more tactical as the formal deployment of U.S. troops in Taiwan or new security guarantees for Taiwan if it were invaded by China. It could also include new rhetoric by Trump during high-level summit visits with Xi regarding U.S. commitments to Taiwan. During his May visit to Beijing, for example, many scholars interpreted some of Trump’s rhetoric on Taiwan as an indication that he was considering adopting a more accommodationist approach with Beijing, at the expense of U.S. support for Taiwan.33 These factors are part of China’s assessment of the overall trendline in U.S.-Taiwan relations, to include high-level visits and exchanges, as well as U.S. arms sales and rhetoric regarding Taiwan.These geopolitical and Taiwan-specific scenarios are factors that might prompt Xi to assess a fundamental change has taken place in the international environment or across the Strait, compelling him to take military action either because Taiwan has crossed Beijing’s “red line” or because a geostrategic window of opportunity has opened while the United States is distracted in other theaters.

Role of U.S. Military Intervention on Taiwan’s behalf (U.S.)

A third key factor in whether Xi believes he can successfully pull off an invasion of Taiwan is his specific assessment of the likelihood that the U.S. military would intervene on Taiwan’s behalf. Here, two factors are most important: first, the rhetoric employed by U.S. presidents regarding Taiwan; and second, the signaling and military posture of the United States Pacific Command (PACOM).On the first factor, U.S. presidents have from time to time made vague statements regarding whether the U.S. military would intervene in a Taiwan scenario, a policy sometimes referred to as “strategic ambiguity.”34 However, a clear break from “strategic ambiguity” may have started under President Joe Biden, who, on two different occasions, stated explicitly and unequivocally that the U.S. military would intervene to support Taiwan were it attacked.35 President Biden’s remarks that the U.S. is willing to get involved militarily to defend Taiwan were widely regarded as a significant deviation from Washington’s long-standing policy of “strategic ambiguity.”Under the Trump administration, Xi is highly attuned to signals from Trump that either reaffirm or depart from this U.S. commitment. Trump has largely maintained the long-standing U.S. policy of strategic ambiguity regarding whether the United States would intervene militarily in the event of a Chinese invasion, having stated in the past that he would not comment on the issue to maintain negotiating leverage.36 But if Trump were to publicly signal that Taiwan could be a bargaining chip during high-level meetings with Xi Jinping, as some assessed he did during their May 2026 meeting, this might lead Xi to conclude that Trump would not come to Taiwan’s aid were China to invade Taipei. This scenario could involve Trump alluding to Taiwan “being a part of China’s territory,” or comparing Xi’s designs on Taiwan to Putin’s designs on Ukraine, for example. Whether intentional or not, such an offhanded rhetorical flourish—which Trump has been known to do—is not completely far-fetched.37Second, the PLA is particularly attuned to public statements, military maneuvers, and overall military posture of the United States’ PACOM, the primary combatant command that oversees a contingency involving China and Taiwan. Were PACOM to undertake a major change of force posture in the Asia-Pacific—such as pulling back troops or reducing its presence in the region, or to signal a new policy of de-emphasizing the U.S. commitment to aid allies and partners in the region— this may provide sufficient justification for Xi and the PLA to conclude that the United States may not be willing to credibly commit to intervening in a conflict over Taiwan.In short, public statements by U.S. presidents over possible U.S. military involvement represent a critical factor to Chinese leaders, since such pledges impact their calculus over whether the PLA would have to actively thwart U.S. military intervention in pursuit of forceful unification of Taiwan. The United States is arguably the only power in the world with the military capability and intent to prevent a successful Chinese invasion, a reality of which Xi Jinping is likely well aware. From China’s perspective, such promises bolster Taiwanese citizens’ confidence in the U.S.’s defense commitment, and may embolden Taiwan’s pursuit of formal independence.

Willingness of U.S. Allies and Partners to Intervene in a Taiwan Scenario (A&P)

Closely related to the previous factor on U.S. support is the role of U.S. allies and partners in directly or indirectly intervening in a Taiwan conflict. While such a role would likely take the form of supporting U.S. operations, rather than direct military intervention, Chinese leaders nonetheless must take into account how and in what fashion U.S. allies may participate in such a scenario, especially as it relates to auxiliary military capabilities. This is important in the context of Xi Jinping’s concern about the involvement of “external forces” in preventing the eventual “reunification” of Taiwan. While he rarely singles out allies such as Japan or Australia by name, his language is intentionally broad enough to encompass all foreign countries that might intervene militarily or politically on Taiwan’s behalf—not just the United States.Japan has been the most forward-leaning U.S. ally when it comes to a Taiwan contingency. Japanese leaders have increasingly framed Taiwan’s security as inextricably linked to that of Japan. Former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe’s formulation that “a Taiwan emergency is a Japanese emergency” reflects a broader consensus in Tokyo that a Taiwan conflict would fundamentally alter Japan’s security environment.38 More recently, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s public remarks in Japan’s Diet, in which she said that if China conducted a naval blockade of Taiwan, it would constitute a “survival-threatening situation” prompting Japan to exercise the right of collective self-defense, is another instance of Japan’s evolution on Taiwan.39Finally, Japanese officials have repeatedly joined U.S. statements opposing unilateral changes to the status quo and emphasizing the importance of peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait.40 However, Japan has not issued a formal pledge to fight, and its likely role is understood as enabling U.S. operations (e.g., basing, logistics, rear-area support) rather than guaranteeing direct combat participation.Australia has also signaled increasing alignment with Washington on the need to maintain peace and buttress deterrence across the Strait. While such statements do not signal an unambiguous pledge to support the United States in a Taiwan scenario, they could be interpreted as reflecting an evolution in Canberra’s thinking over the possibility of supporting a U.S. effort to militarily intervene over Taiwan.41 Senior officials have stressed that Canberra would consult with the United States under the alliance framework rather than automatically commit forces, and Anthony Albanese has refused to answer “hypothetical” questions over Australia’s role in a Taiwan conflict.42 This suggests that even among America’s closest allies, participation would depend on the circumstances, legality, and domestic politics of the conflict. Even so, scholars in Australia and the United States continue to explore how the AUKUS partnership could provide avenues for Australia to support the United States in a Taiwan campaign in ways not contemplated before.43Finally, countries like the Philippines and Singapore may be compelled to support U.S. forces in the Indo-Pacific theater in the event of a war over Taiwan, based on their defense treaties with the United States. At less than 170 kilometers away, the Philippines is particularly vulnerable to a kinetic conflict in the Taiwan Strait. Given this distance, and the existence of its mutual defense treaty with Washington, some scholars posit that the Philippines would get dragged into a conflict by virtue of geographic proximity.44 While Singapore is not a treaty ally of the United States, its close defense partnership with Washington has prompted some to speculate over a possible role in supporting U.S. military assets in the region and assisting with evacuation operations.45These U.S. allies are highlighted because they are the most likely candidates to become involved in a war over Taiwan in support of U.S. operations, both due to their geographic proximity to Taiwan, and, in some cases, because some have begun contemplating Taiwan contingencies with the United States in more discernable ways than before. While South Korea remains a key U.S. ally geographically close to Taiwan, with over 28,000 U.S. troops stationed in the country, the consensus of a majority of scholars and policy-makers is that it is unlikely to play a meaningful role in a Taiwan contingency.46 This is due to South Korea’s primary focus on the threat posed by North Korea, and concerns that involvement in a Taiwan contingency would constitute an unnecessary expenditure of military and political capital.

Taiwanese Deterrent Capabilities (TDC)

The final external factor is China’s assessment of the degree to which Taiwan’s military capabilities and defense spending would prevent or deter military success by Beijing. Here, the central question for Chinese planners is not whether the PLA can defeat Taiwan in aggregate, but whether it can do so rapidly and decisively before Taiwanese resistance hardens or external intervention materializes. Improvements in Taiwan’s defenses can undermine Beijing’s confidence in scoring a rapid fait accompli military campaign by increasing the probability of a protracted war of attrition.Taiwan’s current approach, articulated in its 2025 Quadrennial Defense Review, prioritizes “multi-domain denial and resilient defense,” which is essentially an asymmetric strategy geared towards protraction as opposed to offensive battlefield success. This strategy emphasizes dispersal, survivability, and the ability to maintain operations after initial strikes, and includes investments in mobile anti-ship and air-defense systems, mines, unmanned platforms, hardened command-and-control, and reserve mobilization.47 In this sense, how Taiwan spends on defense is more consequential than how much it spends. If Taiwan can employ asymmetric capabilities that threaten PRC transport ships, ports, and logistics to impose disproportionate costs on Beijing to prolong the conflict, such a strategy has to be taken into account by Chinese leaders and war-planners. Crucially, Taiwan’s capabilities also shape expectations of external support. A force that can survive initial blows and hold out increases the plausibility of U.S. or allied intervention, thereby compounding Chinese uncertainty.Ultimately, Taiwan’s military posture influences Beijing’s calculus by eroding confidence in speed, lowering expectations of decisive success, and raising the perceived risks of escalation and protraction. These are factors that in the minds of Chinese leaders can deter any decision to invade—not by denying the possibility of outright victory, but by casting doubt on the feasibility of achieving it on terms acceptable to Beijing.

IV. Interaction of Variables

The variables outlined above interact with one another in ways that can either raise or lower Beijing’s perceived incentives to use force. It is beyond the scope of this paper to cover all the various permutations in which the factors in this framework can interact to influence leaders’ decision-making. However, a few general observations can be made.First, PLA readiness is arguably the most important enabling variable because it determines whether Chinese leaders believe military action is operationally feasible. Without sufficient confidence in the PLA’s ability to execute a complex joint campaign, other variables, such as Taiwan’s political trajectory or doubts about U.S. resolve, may increase frustration in Beijing but are unlikely by themselves to produce a decision to invade. PLA readiness, however, is not sufficient on its own. A highly capable PLA does not automatically mean that Xi Jinping would choose war. It only makes the military option more credible and therefore more available.Second, several variables function as prerequisites or threshold conditions. Domestic stability is one such condition. A relatively stable domestic environment gives Chinese leaders greater confidence that they can absorb the economic, diplomatic, and political costs of a Taiwan conflict, including sanctions, market disruption, and possible escalation with outside powers. Conversely, severe domestic instability could either constrain Beijing by raising fears of internal backlash or, in more extreme circumstances, create incentives for Chinese leaders to take greater risks if they believe nationalist mobilization could reinforce regime legitimacy. Similarly, perceptions of Taiwan’s permanent separation from the mainland are best understood as a political threshold variable. If Beijing concludes that peaceful unification is still plausible over the long term, the incentive to use force may remain limited. But if Chinese leaders come to believe that Taiwan is moving irreversibly toward permanent separation, the perceived cost of inaction could rise sharply.Third, the most dangerous scenario is the convergence of several mutually reinforcing conditions. A particularly destabilizing combination would involve high PLA readiness; growing Chinese perceptions that Taiwan is moving irreversibly away from unification; declining expectations of U.S. military intervention; limited anticipated participation by U.S. allies and partners; and weakened confidence in Taiwan’s ability to resist long enough for outside support to arrive. In such a scenario, Beijing might conclude that both the necessity and feasibility of military action have increased at the same time. The “necessity” side of the equation would be driven by fears that the political window for unification is closing. The “feasibility” side would be driven by confidence that the PLA can achieve rapid success before outside actors can intervene.These variables can also compound one another. For example, Taiwanese deterrent capabilities affect not only Beijing’s assessment of Taiwan itself, but also its expectations about U.S. and allied intervention. If Taiwan can survive initial strikes and prolong a conflict, Chinese leaders may assume that the United States and its partners would have more time and political space to intervene. By contrast, if Beijing believes Taiwan’s defenses are brittle, then the perceived likelihood of a successful fait accompli rises. Similarly, U.S. resolve shapes allied behavior: if Washington appears hesitant or divided, Beijing may infer that Japan, Australia, the Philippines, and other partners would be even less likely to assume major risks. In this sense, perceptions of U.S. resolve condition Beijing’s expectations about the broader coalition response.Finally, the variables may interact differently depending on whether Beijing sees time as working for or against China. If Chinese leaders believe the balance of power is continuing to shift in their favor, they may prefer patience, coercion, and political warfare over military action. But if they believe China is approaching the peak of its relative advantage, at the same time that Taiwan’s identity hardens, U.S.-Taiwan ties deepen, and allied coordination improves, then the same variables could produce a closing-window logic. Under those conditions, China may become most dangerous not when it feels fully confident, but when it believes that a favorable opportunity is closing. Thus, the central analytical contribution of this framework is that the likelihood of Chinese military action depends less on any single trigger than on Beijing’s overall perception that the balance of urgency, capability, and acceptable risk has shifted decisively in favor of using force.

V. Conclusion

This paper seeks to introduce a set of variables for academics and policymakers interested in assessing the likely factors that matter to Chinese leaders when contemplating the use of force to resolve the Taiwan question. The intent is not to offer an exhaustive or comprehensive list of all factors that matter, but rather to explore the factors of most consequence to China. The factors identified here are intended to be somewhat time and leader-agnostic—meaning they should stand the test of time irrespective of which leader is in charge in China (or the United States and Taiwan, for that matter). But as with all methodological endeavors, future events and the evolution of military capabilities will inevitably require adjustments.Given those caveats, looking out into the future, one might argue that if the PRC is confident that U.S. and Taiwanese military capabilities will continue to decline relative to China’s in cross-Strait scenarios, and that U.S. resolve to intervene is weakening, the CCP leadership may adopt a more relaxed approach. On the other hand, if CCP leaders believe that China has already reached the top of its relative power, they could decide that there is a limited window of opportunity to reunify. The United States, at some point in the coming decade, may reorient its military posture away from the Indo-Pacific; China might suffer a serious economic downturn coupled with unfavorable demographics; and new military technologies and systems may emerge, such as AI, that will fundamentally alter the calculus of future leaders in Beijing. These are all scenarios that must be considered.Taiwan, if persuaded that the United States was disengaging militarily from the Western Pacific, might become willing to compromise and begin substantive talks with the PRC more on the CCP’s terms, or it could strive to increase its own defensive capabilities and seek other security partners, though this would be a difficult task since in at least this instance, the United States seems to be the indispensable nation.Conversely, Xi and the PLA may lose patience with Taiwan. Signs of this occurring could include rhetorical shifts in public speeches by Xi or senior CCP officials, such as the removal of the word “peaceful” from China’s “peaceful reunification” formula for Taiwan; a new white paper or policy document on Taiwan that emphasizes a closing window for peaceful resolution of the Taiwan question; or more pronounced, destabilizing military exercises or maneuvers near Taiwan that would push Taiwan or the United States to respond.48Finally, a long-term factor in Chinese domestic politics is how Xi’s new wave of purges could affect the PLA’s readiness going forward.49 The purges themselves are likely to slow some weapons modernization programs, disrupt command structures and decision-making, and weaken morale—all of which would degrade the PLA’s ability to fight in the near to medium term.50 In the years ahead, the purges raise fundamental questions regarding whether Beijing will be forced to exercise greater caution before pursuing large-scale military operations, such as an amphibious assault on Taiwan, or whether Xi will become impatient with PLA readiness concerns in such a fashion that would prompt him to launch an invasion as a “test” of PLA capabilities.
